# English for Journalists

### *International Edition · Book 2*

**Across Borders**
Student's Book
*A free press, without borders.*
CEFR lower B1 → medium B1   ·   10 units   ·   Atlas Wire, and the newsrooms it works with

> **A note on real and invented content.** The facts about journalism around the world in 2026 are true, dated and attributed on the page. Atlas Wire, Kalina Daily, the River Basin Network, the Meridian Post, their staff, the town of Kalina, the river Vara and the people in the stories are invented, for practice. Real people and real outlets are only ever in true, sourced facts — never in an invented quote.


---


### WELCOME · About Book 2

English for Journalists, Book 2, continues the newsroom English course. In Book 1, you learned to report a story with Atlas Wire, an invented independent news agency with a world desk in Geneva, and to carry it from the crossing at Kalina to a front page. In Book 2, that story grows: Atlas Wire begins to work with other newsrooms — Kalina Daily, the local paper in the town itself; the River Basin Network, a regional network; and the Meridian Post, a large international daily — and learns to make one story with partners who are bigger and smaller than itself, in English, without losing anybody's truth.
The course climbs from lower B1 to medium B1 — the first half of B1. Each unit teaches one new piece of grammar and one part of cross-border journalism: recapping a running story, briefing a colleague abroad, planning across time zones, filing to a foreign desk, setting the conditions for publication, weighing a claim, writing for the wire, explaining a place to a distant reader, co-writing, and finally co-producing a package for the world.

**The cross-border strand**

About a fifth of the book is the **Across Borders** strand: in every unit, at least one part involves working with a partner in another country, and Units 4, 7 and 10 are wholly cross-border. It prepares a journalist to work inside an international partnership — with the outlets above them, who reach further, and the outlets below them, whose story it is.

**How to use this book**

1. Each unit has a Warm-Up and eleven parts: Words, Grammar, a Skill, Listening, Reading, Writing, Speaking, Ethics, Digital, Review, and an Assignment.
2. Every part builds up step by step: you see a model, notice how it works, practise it, and then produce your own.
3. Grammar is taught half as controlled practice and half in your own words. Every part mixes exercises you can check with open tasks to discuss and create.
4. The Ethics part in every unit builds the Code — accurate, fair, independent, and kind — now tested across borders, and in both directions.
5. The Answer Key at the end of each unit gives the answers to the closed exercises. Open tasks (discussion, role-play, and your own writing) are marked.

**The newsroom, and the newsrooms it works with**

**Where we are now.** A year has passed since Atlas Wire published its front page, *A crossing comes home*. The valley has changed, the story has run all year — and now the coverage has been noticed well beyond the wire. This week, a message arrived from Omar Faris, an editor at the Meridian Post, a large international daily. Atlas Wire has never co-produced a story with another newsroom before. (The Meridian Post and Omar Faris are invented, for practice.)

### PART 1 · The words of a running story

*The words for a story that grows and travels. Learn these first.*

> **[FIGURE: `u1-words`]** — *Four key words — coverage, running story, reach, pick up.*

**The words**

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| coverage | the reporting of a story |
| running story | a story that continues over time |
| cover | to report on a story |
| follow up | to report more on a story |
| pick up | when another outlet takes your story |
| reach | how many people see your work |
| audience | the people who read or watch |
| outlet | a paper, network, agency or website |
| syndicate | to share or sell a story to other outlets |
| update | new information |
| so far | until now |
| recently | a short time ago |
| propose | to suggest |
| partner | an outlet you work with |
| co-production | a piece made by two or more outlets together |

### PART 2 · Grammar: perfect and past

*Present perfect for up to now; past simple for a finished time.*

> **[FIGURE: `u1-gA`]** — *present perfect = up to now · past simple = a finished time.*

> **1 · Present perfect — up to now**
>
> Form: {{has / have}} + past participle.
> We use it for experience and unfinished time: We {{have covered}} this story {{for}} a year. The Meridian Post {{has just}} contacted us.
> Signal words: {{for, since, just, already, yet, ever, never}}.

> **2 · Past simple — a finished time**
>
> Form: the past form of the verb (regular {{-ed}}, or irregular).
> We use it for a finished time: The crossing {{reopened}} last spring. Omar {{wrote}} to us last week.
> Signal words: [[last week, ago, yesterday, in April]].

> **[FIGURE: `u1-gB`]** — *just, already, yet, ever, never — all with the present perfect.*

> **3 · Which one?**
>
> Result now, or up to now → present perfect: "We {{have worked}} on it for a year."
> A finished time → past simple: "We {{started}} it last April."
> *Ever* and *never* ask and answer about experience: "{{Have}} you {{ever}} co-produced a story? — No, {{never}}."

> **[FIGURE: `u1-gC`]** — *for + a length of time; since + a point in time.*

### PART 5 · Reading: a year on

*Two readings. Read for the whole year, and for how to catch up.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-reach`]** — *A year of coverage — and a story that has travelled.*

**Reading A** · a year on: the story that travelled

> **A year on: the story that travelled**
>
> It has been a year since Atlas Wire published its front page about the crossing at Kalina, and the story has never really stopped. It has become the desk's longest running story, and, this month, it has reached further than anyone expected.
> A great deal has happened since that front page. The crossing reopened last spring, and, according to the Crossing Office, a hundred families have returned to the valley. The school reopened in the autumn, and a small café has opened at the end of the bridge. Atlas Wire has followed every step, and its correspondent, Mira Sandoval, has written most of the coverage.
> "I have covered this valley for a year now," Mira said. "When we started, the road was empty. I never thought the story would travel so far. But it has — people have read it in countries that have never heard of the river Vara."
> Last week, that reach became clear. An editor at the Meridian Post, a large international daily, wrote to the desk. He said he had followed the coverage for months, and he proposed working together. Atlas Wire has never co-produced a story with another newsroom before.
> "We are an agency; we file, and others publish," said Ana Ferreira, the editor-in-chief. "We have not agreed anything yet. But the story has grown, and it has found a much wider audience. Now we have to decide, carefully, what to do next — and how to keep it honest."
> The Post is not the only outlet that has noticed. In recent weeks, the River Basin Network has asked to run the coverage across the region, and readers have written from four continents. The audience, once a wire list, has grown far wider than before.
> There is one more thing the desk has not forgotten. Kalina Daily, the small paper in the town itself, has covered the crossing every week since long before Atlas Wire arrived. "Whatever we build," Ana said, "they are in it, and their name is on it. That part is not negotiable."

> **[FIGURE: `g-partners`]** — *A long-running story can reach far beyond the town where it began.*

**Reading B** · catching up on a running story — four tips

> **Four tips for a recap**
>
> **1. Say what has happened so far.** Use the present perfect for the whole story up to now: 'We have covered it for a year.'
> **2. Say what happened at key moments.** Use the past simple for a finished time: 'The crossing reopened last spring.'
> **3. Say what is new.** Use *just*, *recently* and *already*: 'A daily has just noticed our work.' Keep it short.
> **4. Name your sources, and stay accurate.** A recap is still journalism: a source for each number, no more than has really happened, and the name of the newsroom that was there before you.
> **5. Keep it short.** A recap is a bridge, not the story. Give enough to understand where things stand, and no more.

### PART 8 · Ethics: keeping it accurate, keeping it ours

*A story that travels must stay accurate — and stay true to the place it comes from.*

> **[FIGURE: `u1-ethA`]** — *'Fully recovered' is a claim; 'has improved a lot' is what you can say.*

**A first case** · the recap that says too much

> **A case.** Mira writes a recap for the new partner. She wants it to sound strong, so she nearly writes: 'The Kalina valley has fully recovered, and everything is finished.' It would read well, and a big partner might like a simple, bright line. But that is not accurate. The crossing has reopened and many families have returned — a great deal has improved — but the clinic is still closed, the bus does not cross yet, and not everyone has come home. The partner has never been to Kalina; they will build their whole picture on Mira's words. A recap is still journalism, and its first reader trusts it completely. Mira knows the Code: report what has really happened, not more. What does Mira write in the recap?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

**8A**  Choose (a) or (b), and write one reason.

1. (a) 'the valley has fully recovered'  (b) 'the valley has improved a lot, but work remains'.   Choice: ______  Because ________________________
2. Saying 'fully recovered' when it is not is (a) accurate  (b) not accurate.   Choice: ______

**8B**  Can you say it has happened? Write Y (yes) or N (not yet).

2. Everyone has returned. ______
3. Many families have come back. ______
4. The valley has fully recovered. ______

**PRACTISE** — Apply the Code

> A ______ is still journalism. Be ______ : do not say ______ has happened than really has, and ______ every number.

**PRODUCE** — Discuss

**8D**  Discuss. Why is a 'too positive' recap a problem, especially for a partner who has never seen the valley?

**A second case** · keeping the local voice

> **[FIGURE: `u1-ethB`]** — *A bigger partner's reach is welcome — but the story stays true to the place.*

> **A case.** The Meridian Post is interested — but the editor suggests a simpler, more dramatic angle: 'the miracle valley that came back from nothing'. It would travel well and reach millions. But it is not quite true. The recovery was slow and hard, and it was done, day by day, by the people who live there. 'Came back from nothing' erases years of ordinary work, and it makes the valley sound helpless rather than strong. There is a second problem: the Post's draft names only Atlas Wire, and Kalina Daily has covered this crossing every week for years. The Post's reach is real and welcome. But the facts, and the credit, are not the Post's to change. The Code says: independence — a partner's reach must never change the story, however large the audience. What does Atlas Wire do?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

## BOOK 2 · UNIT 2 · The Backstory: How Things Used to Be

**Beat · Feature & Across Borders**  ·  CEFR lower B1 → medium B1

**In this unit you learn to…**

1. describe how things used to be (used to)
2. talk about repeated past actions (would)
3. use the past continuous for background
4. give the backstory to a colleague abroad

> **[FIGURE: `g-team`]** — *The Atlas Wire team — now telling the valley's backstory to a much wider audience.*

**An editor asks for the backstory.** The Meridian Post was not the only outlet to notice Atlas Wire's coverage. Omar Faris is now helping bring the story to readers on four continents. But to tell it well, he needs the backstory — how Kalina used to be, before the barrier came down and the families left. This week, Mira writes that backstory, and briefs Omar. Dren, at Kalina Daily, has the part no outsider has: he lived it. (Kalina Daily, the Meridian Post, Dren and Omar are invented, for practice.)


---

### WARM-UP · The way it was

*A short scene to start the unit. Read it, then answer.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-meeting`]** — *The morning conference — the team remembers how the valley used to be.*

> "Omar has asked for background," Ana says. "He wants to know what the valley was like before." Mira nods. "Dren remembers it better than any of us. The bridge used to be full every morning. Old Bekim would open his stall at dawn and sweep the boards. Then, over one hard winter, families began to leave. When the barrier came down, the road was emptying, week by week."
> She pauses. "For seven years it was quiet. But that quiet is the backstory — it is why the reopening matters so much. Omar needs to understand the before, or he cannot understand the now."

### PART 1 · The words of the backstory

*The words for background and memory. Learn these first.*

> **[FIGURE: `u2-words`]** — *Four key words — background, context, backstory, brief.*

**The words**

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| background | the facts behind a story |
| context | what helps you understand a story |
| backstory | what happened before the story began |
| brief (v) | to give someone the key facts |
| brief (n) | a short set of key facts |
| in those days | at that time in the past |
| quiet | with little noise or activity |
| empty | with no people |
| busy | full of activity |
| rebuild | to build again |
| return | to come back |
| memory | something you remember |
| recall | to remember |
| no longer | not any more |
| once | at a time in the past |
| back then | at that time |
| correspondent | a reporter who files from another place |
| archive | the record of what an outlet has published |

### PART 2 · Grammar: the way things were

*used to for past states and habits; would for repeated actions; the past continuous for background.*

> **[FIGURE: `u2-gA`]** — *used to — a past state that is not true now; would — a repeated action.*

> **1 · used to — how things were**
>
> Form: {{used to}} + verb. The bridge {{used to be}} closed. Families {{used to live}} on both sides.
> For a past state or habit that is not true now.
> Negative: It [[didn't use to]] be busy. Question: [[Did]] it [[use to]] be quiet?

> **2 · would — what happened again and again**
>
> Form: {{would}} + verb. Every morning, Bekim {{would open}} his stall.
> For a repeated past action — something that happened again and again.
> [[Not for states]]: say *it used to be closed*, NOT *it would be closed*.

> **[FIGURE: `u2-gB`]** — *past continuous = the longer background; past simple = the event.*

> **3 · past continuous — the background**
>
> Form: {{was / were}} + verb{{-ing}}. The families {{were leaving}} when the barrier came down.
> For a longer background action, often interrupted by a past-simple event.
> Set the scene: "It {{was raining}}, and the road {{was}} quiet."

> **[FIGURE: `u2-gC`]** — *State, scene, or event — each has its own form.*

### PART 5 · Reading: the way it was

*Two readings. Read for the backstory, and for how to give good background.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-reach`]** — *A backstory feature — the valley, before the story we know.*

**Reading A** · the backstory: how the crossing used to be

> **Before the quiet: a short history of the Kalina crossing**
>
> To understand the reopening of the Kalina crossing, you have to know the bridge as it used to be. For years, this was one of the busiest crossings on the river. It was never rich, but it was full of life, and everyone knew everyone on both banks.
> In those days, the market on the bridge opened before the sun. Stall-holders like Bekim would arrive at dawn, set out the boxes, and sweep the boards. By seven, the crossing was loud with sellers and buyers from both sides. Children would cut across on their way to the school on the far bank, and old men would sit outside the café at the end of the bridge, as they had for thirty years.
> Then, over one hard winter, things began to change. Families were leaving, quietly at first, and then in greater numbers. Stalls closed one by one. "I remember it clearly," Bekim says. "One morning I was sweeping the boards, and I looked up. The bridge was empty. I had never seen it empty before."
> When the barrier finally came down, the valley went quiet, and it stayed quiet for seven years. The café shut. Grass grew between the stones at the end of the bridge. For a long time, Kalina was a place people remembered rather than a place people crossed.
> That is the backstory, and it is not decoration: it matters. The crossing that reopened last spring did not open in an empty history; it opened where a whole life used to be. When a hundred families return, the number means little on its own. It means a great deal when you know how many left, and how long the valley waited. The past is not just background. It is the reason the present is news.

> **[FIGURE: `g-partners`]** — *The backstory is what lets a distant reader feel the weight of the news.*

**Reading B** · good background: what an editor abroad needs

> **Four rules for good background**
>
> **1. Use used to for how things were.** Past states and habits that are not true now: 'The market used to be busy.'
> **2. Use would for what people did again and again.** Repeated actions: 'Every morning, he would open his stall.' (But not for states.)
> **3. Use the past continuous to set the scene.** A longer background, often broken by an event: 'Families were leaving when the barrier came down.'
> **4. Keep it fair and in order.** Give the background in the order it happened, and never make the past worse or better than it was to make today bigger. Where you can, take it from someone who was there — and say who.

### PART 8 · Ethics: a fair backstory

*The past is powerful. A fair backstory tells it as it was — not worse, and not like a fairy tale.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-code`]** — *The Code applies to the past as much as to today: the backstory must be accurate, honest and fair.*

> **[FIGURE: `u2-ethA`]** — *A backstory can be true, or it can be shaped to make today look bigger.*

**A first case** · making the past sound worse

> **A case.** Mira wants the reopening to feel like a triumph, so she is tempted to darken the backstory: to write that the valley 'used to be a place of nothing but fear and ruin.' It would make the recovery look bigger. But it is not true. The valley used to be poor, yes, and the quiet years were real — but before them it was an ordinary, living place, full of small joys: children crossing to school, coffee carried over the bridge at dawn, neighbours on two banks who knew each other. To paint the past as 'nothing but ruin' would erase those people and their ordinary lives, just to make a brighter headline today. The Code says: report the past as it was. What does Mira write?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

**8D**  Discuss. Why does erasing the ordinary good of the past also hurt the people who lived it?

**A second case** · the fairy-tale angle

> **[FIGURE: `u2-ethB`]** — *A partner abroad may want a simpler, prettier past. Keep it true.*

> **A case.** Omar's own editor at the Meridian Post loves the backstory, but suggests a softer, prettier version for an international audience: 'the little paradise that was lost and found again.' It is warm and it would travel well. But it is not quite true. Kalina was never a paradise; it was an ordinary crossing, sometimes hard, made of real people. 'Paradise lost' turns them into a fairy tale, and a fairy tale is easy to forget. The Post's reach is real, and Mira wants the story to travel — but the people in it deserve to be seen as they were, and Dren, who grew up there, would not recognise the place in that sentence. The Code says: keep it true, even when a prettier version would please a partner. What does Mira tell Omar?

**Beat · Planning & Across Borders**  ·  CEFR lower B1 → medium B1

**In this unit you learn to…**

1. make plans and promises with will
2. talk about plans already made with going to
3. use the present continuous for fixed arrangements

> **[FIGURE: `g-team`]** — *The Atlas Wire team — planning a project that will run in four countries at once.*

**Three outlets, one project.** The backstory did its work: readers abroad now see why one crossing matters. So the story grows. Atlas Wire, Kalina Daily, the River Basin Network and the Meridian Post are going to cover the whole Vara basin together — the other crossings, what reopened and what did not. Four newsrooms, four clocks, one plan. (Atlas Wire, Kalina Daily, the River Basin Network and the Meridian Post are invented, for practice.)

### PART 1 · The words of planning

*The words for plans, dates and deadlines. Learn these first.*

> **[FIGURE: `u3-words`]** — *Four key words — plan, schedule, deadline, time zone.*

**The words**

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| plan (n) | what you are going to do, and when |
| schedule | a list of times for the work |
| deadline | the time by which work must be finished |
| time zone | the local clock in one part of the world |
| coordinate | to make people's work fit together |
| assignment | work given to a reporter |
| commission (v) | to ask someone to do work for you |
| pitch (v) | to offer an idea to an editor |
| draft (n) | an early version of a text |
| agree | to decide together |
| diary | the list of planned stories |
| slot | where and when a story will run |
| lead time | the time you need before publication |
| available | free to meet or to work |
| confirm | to say something is certain |
| kick-off | a project's first meeting |
| milestone | a date when one part must be done |
| ahead | in front, in time or place |

### PART 2 · Grammar: talking about the future

*will for decisions and promises; going to for plans already made; the present continuous for fixed arrangements.*

> **[FIGURE: `u3-gA`]** — *will — a decision at the moment of speaking; going to — a plan made before.*

> **1 · will — decisions, promises, predictions**
>
> Form: {{will}} + verb. "I {{will move}} the call to four." "It {{will take}} three weeks."
> For a decision made as you speak, a promise, an offer, or a prediction.
> Negative: It [[won't]] be ready. Question: [[Will]] you file by Friday?

> **2 · going to — a plan already made**
>
> Form: {{am / is / are going to}} + verb. "We {{are going to cover}} the whole basin."
> For a plan or intention decided before now — and for a prediction you can see coming.
> [[Not a decision at the moment of speaking]]: for that, use *will*.

> **[FIGURE: `u3-gB`]** — *going to = the plan; present continuous = the plan with a time and a place.*

> **3 · present continuous — a fixed arrangement**
>
> Form: {{am / is / are}} + verb{{-ing}}, with a future time. "We {{are publishing}} on Sunday."
> For an arrangement that is fixed: a time, a place, and other people who know.
> "Ines {{is joining}} at four." "Dren {{is travelling}} on Thursday."

> **[FIGURE: `u3-gC`]** — *Decision now, plan already made, or fixed arrangement — each has its own form.*

### PART 3 · Planning across time zones

*A cross-border plan needs one calendar, one deadline, and a time that works for everybody.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-timezones`]** — *Four partners, four clocks. Somebody's convenient hour is somebody's dawn.*

> **[FIGURE: `u3-skill`]** — *A good plan says who, what, when — and in whose time zone.*

**MODEL** — A model plan

> "Here is the plan. We are going to cover the whole Vara basin — seven crossings, not one. Kalina Daily is reporting the two upstream; the River Basin Network is taking the middle three; we are taking the mouth of the river. The Meridian Post is editing the English version.
> The kick-off call is on Thursday at 16:00 Geneva — 10:00 for Omar, 18:00 for Ines. First drafts are due on the 14th. We are publishing on the last Sunday, all four of us, at 07:00 GMT. I will send the calendar tonight."

**NOTICE** — Notice the plan

> **[FIGURE: `u3-read`]** — *Every milestone has a date; every date has a time zone.*

**MODEL** — Audio 3.1 — Ana, Ines and Omar

> **Ana:**  Thank you both for the early hour. We are going to cover the whole basin — seven crossings.

> **Ana:**  The 14th. Then we have eight days to edit and translate.

> **Omar:**  Understood. I will send the embargo note tomorrow.

### PART 5 · Reading: one basin, four newsrooms

*Two readings. Read for the plan, and for how to plan across borders.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-reach`]** — *One project, four mastheads, four audiences — and a single hour of publication.*

**Reading A** · the project plan, explained

> **Seven crossings, one Sunday: how the basin project will work**
>
> At the end of this month, four newsrooms are publishing one investigation at the same hour. It is called *The Seven Crossings*, and it asks a simple question: a year after Kalina reopened, what has happened to the rest of the river?
> The work is divided by geography. Kalina Daily, the paper in the town itself, is reporting the two upstream crossings. The River Basin Network is taking the middle three. Atlas Wire is covering the two at the mouth of the river, and the Meridian Post is editing the English version.
> "Nobody could do this alone, and nobody should," says Ines Duarte, who edits for the River Basin Network. "We are going to put seven small stories beside each other, and the picture they make is the story."
> The calendar is short. First drafts are due on the 14th; the edit and translation take eight days; everything goes out at 07:00 GMT on the last Sunday. "That hour is the only thing we will not move," says Ana Ferreira of Atlas Wire. "If one partner runs early, the others lose the day."
> Four time zones have their own rules. The kick-off call was moved twice: four o'clock in Geneva is ten in the morning for the Post's desk and six in the evening for Dren Markaj at Kalina Daily. "We learned to write the time zone beside every hour," Omar Faris of the Meridian Post says. "It sounds small. It saves a week."
> The hardest part, all four editors say, is not the logistics. It is holding to one standard when four newsrooms have four house styles, four lawyers and four audiences. So the partners agreed their rules before their deadlines: every figure confirmed twice, every local reporter named, and nothing published that the others have not seen.

> **[FIGURE: `g-partners`]** — *Four newsrooms, one standard: the rules come before the calendar.*

**Reading B** · good planning across borders

> **Four rules for planning with partners**
>
> **1. Name the time zone every time.** Write '16:00 Geneva' or '07:00 GMT', never just 'four o'clock'. A plan that does not say whose clock it means is not a plan.
> **2. Share the calendar, not only the deadline.** Partners need the milestones between: the kick-off, the drafts, the edit, the hour.
> **3. Agree the standard before the schedule.** How a figure is confirmed, who is named, what each partner may publish — all before anyone writes.
> **4. Let the smallest partner choose the hour.** The newsroom closest to the story has the fewest people and the least room to move. It should not be the one getting up at dawn.

### PART 8 · Ethics: a plan you can keep

*A date is a promise. Promising one you cannot keep costs somebody else the work.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-code`]** — *A plan is part of the Code: what you promise a partner, you owe them.*

> **[FIGURE: `u3-ethA`]** — *A partner's perfect date can be another newsroom's impossible one.*

**A first case** · the date that suits the biggest partner

> **A case.** The Meridian Post wants to publish a week earlier, so the project lands in its big Sunday edition. Omar asks Mira: can Atlas Wire be ready? She wants to say yes — the Post's reach is enormous, and a partner who is pleased comes back. But a week earlier means Priya cannot confirm the water-level figures twice, and Dren cannot reach the far-bank families at all. The thin part would be the part about the people whose river it is. The Code says: do not promise a date that forces you to publish what you have not checked. What does Mira tell Omar?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

**A second case** · the call nobody could attend

> **[FIGURE: `u3-ethB`]** — *A decision taken while one partner was offline is not an agreement.*

> **A case.** The second kick-off call falls at an hour when Dren is on the road and cannot join. The three larger partners take it anyway, and agree how the upstream crossings will be framed — his crossings, in his town. Afterwards, the minutes say 'agreed by all partners'. Nobody lied; Dren was simply not there. But Kalina Daily is the smallest partner, closest to the people in the story, and it will still be in Kalina long after the others have moved on. The Code says: a partner who could not be in the room has not agreed. What should Mira do?

## BOOK 2 · UNIT 4 · Across the Desk: Reporting What Was Said

**Beat · Across Borders (wholly)**  ·  CEFR lower B1 → medium B1

**In this unit you learn to…**

1. report what someone said (reported speech)
2. use say and tell correctly
3. attribute a fact with according to
4. file copy to a desk in another country

> **[FIGURE: `g-team`]** — *The Atlas Wire team — filing to a foreign desk, where every quote is checked again.*

**A quote crosses four borders.** This unit is wholly cross-border. A woman speaks at a stall in Kalina, in her own language. Dren writes it down. Mira reports it to Omar's desk at the Meridian Post, in English. A subeditor in another city tidies it for print. By the time a reader on another continent sees it, the sentence has crossed four borders — and it has to arrive meaning exactly what she meant. (Atlas Wire, Kalina Daily, the Meridian Post and everyone in the stories are invented, for practice.)

### PART 1 · The words of attribution

*The words for quoting, reporting and saying where a fact came from.*

> **[FIGURE: `u4-words`]** — *Four key words — quote, paraphrase, attribution, according to.*

**The words**

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| quote (n) | a person's exact words |
| paraphrase (v) | to report what was said in your own words |
| attribution | the name you put beside a fact |
| attribute (v) | to say where a fact came from |
| according to | as said by a person or body |
| on the record | said for publication, with a name |
| off the record | said not for publication |
| desk | the editors who handle one kind of story |
| file (v) | to send your story to the desk |
| copy (n) | the text a reporter files |
| subeditor | the editor who checks and cuts copy |
| translate | to put words into another language |
| interpreter | a person who translates speech |
| accurate | exactly right |
| claim (v) | to say something is true without proof |
| deny | to say something is not true |
| insist | to say something firmly again |
| add | to say something more |

### PART 2 · Grammar: reporting what was said

*Reported speech and the tense shift; say and tell; according to for facts.*

> **[FIGURE: `u4-gA`]** — *Direct speech keeps the words; reported speech shifts the tense back.*

> **1 · reported speech — one step back**
>
> Direct: "The water {{is}} better." → Reported: She said the water {{was}} better.
> Present → past · past → past perfect · {{will}} → {{would}} · {{can}} → {{could}}
> Pronouns and times move too: *today* → {{that day}}, *tomorrow* → {{the next day}}.

> **2 · say and tell**
>
> {{say}} + what was said: She [[said]] the water was better. ([[not]] *she said me*)
> {{tell}} + person + what was said: She [[told me]] the water was better.
> Also: *add*, *insist*, *deny*, *claim* — each carries a different weight. Choose carefully.

> **[FIGURE: `u4-gB`]** — *say something · tell somebody something — the difference matters in print.*

> **3 · according to — attributing a fact**
>
> Form: {{According to}} + a person or body + a fact. "{{According to}} the Crossing Office, 112 families have returned."
> Use it for a fact you have not confirmed yourself, and for figures from an official body.
> [[Not for your own reporting]]: if you counted it, say so.

> **[FIGURE: `u4-gC`]** — *Quote, paraphrase, or according to — three ways to carry what was said.*

### PART 5 · Reading: how a quote travels

*Two readings. Read for the journey of a sentence, and for the rules that protect it.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-reach`]** — *One sentence, four newsrooms, millions of readers. It has to arrive intact.*

**Reading A** · a sentence crosses four borders

> **The long way round: how one sentence reached print**
>
> The sentence began at a stall on the Kalina bridge, early on a Tuesday. A woman selling apples was asked how the river was this year, and she answered, in her own language, that the water was a little better than last year.
> Dren Markaj of Kalina Daily wrote the words down twice: once as she said them, once in English. "The first version is the evidence," he says. "The second is only my best attempt."
> Mira Sandoval of Atlas Wire read the English back to the woman before they left the bridge. The woman agreed with it. That took ninety seconds, and it is the reason the sentence survived everything that came next.
> The copy went to the Meridian Post's foreign desk, where a subeditor met it for the first time. She had never been to Kalina and could not call the woman. What she had was the copy, and the copy said who had spoken, in which language, and who had interpreted.
> Her first instinct was to shorten. 'The water is a little better this year' is nine words; 'the river has recovered' is four, and it reads better. She queried it. Mira said no, and explained why: the woman had made a small, careful claim about one year, and the shorter version made a large claim about a river.
> "A desk abroad has to be able to trust the copy, because it cannot check the stall," says Omar Faris, who edits the project at the Post. "So we do not improve quotes. We query them."
> The sentence ran as she said it, with her name, her town, and a line saying the interview was conducted in her own language. Four newsrooms, four editors, two languages — and nine words that still meant what she meant.

> **[FIGURE: `g-partners`]** — *Partners do not improve each other's quotes. They query them.*

**Reading B** · reporting what was said

> **Four rules for reported speech**
>
> **1. Shift the tense, not the meaning.** 'The water is better' becomes *she said the water was better*. The tense moves back one step; the claim stays the same size.
> **2. Say who, and how you know.** *Said* and *told* for speech, *according to* for a fact you did not confirm. Name the person or body every time.
> **3. Never improve a quote.** A tidier sentence is a different sentence. If a quote is long, cut it with care, or paraphrase it and say that you have.
> **4. Carry the language with the words.** Say which language it was spoken in, say who interpreted, and read the English back to the speaker.

### PART 8 · Ethics: the size of a claim

*A reported sentence can be made bigger or smaller without a single word being invented. That is the danger.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-code`]** — *Accuracy is not only about facts. It is about the size of what someone said.*

> **[FIGURE: `u4-ethA`]** — *'A little better' and 'recovered' are both true-sounding. Only one is true.*

**A first case** · the tidier sentence

> **A case.** The Post's subeditor is not trying to mislead anybody. She has nine words that read awkwardly and four that read well, and 'the river has recovered' is the kind of line a reader remembers. She does not invent anything: she is reporting what residents say. But the woman made a small claim about one year, and the short version makes a large claim about a river. If the water falls again next summer, the woman will be the one who said it had recovered. The Code says: a paraphrase must carry the same weight as the words. What does Mira tell the desk?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

**8A**  Choose (a) or (b), and write one reason.

1. (a) 'residents say the river has recovered'  (b) 'the water is a little better this year'.   Choice: ______  Because ________________________
2. Making a quote shorter and larger is (a) good editing  (b) a change of claim.   Choice: ______

**8B**  Same size, or bigger? Write S or B.

1. 'She said the water was a little better.' ______
2. 'Residents say the river has recovered.' ______
3. 'According to the Crossing Office, 112 families have returned.' ______
4. 'Hundreds are pouring back, officials say.' ______

**PRACTISE** — Apply the Code

> Keep the ______ of the claim. Put a ______ beside every fact. Do not ______ a quote. Read a translation ______ to the speaker.

**A second case** · the interview that was not ours

> **[FIGURE: `u4-ethB`]** — *A partner's interview is theirs. Carrying it is not the same as owning it.*

> **A case.** Dren told Mira on a call what the man at the lorry park had said. He said it as a colleague, thinking aloud, not as copy — and the man had refused to be named. Later, the Post's desk asks Mira for 'anything on the lorries'. She could write 'Kalina Daily reported that the lorries were returning'. Nobody would be lying: Dren is a reporter, and he did say it. But he said it to her, not in print, and the man behind it never agreed to anything. The Code says: what a colleague tells you is not published by being repeated. What does Mira send the desk?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

## BOOK 2 · UNIT 5 · If We Confirm It: The Conditions for Publishing

**Beat · Verification & Across Borders**  ·  CEFR lower B1 → medium B1

**In this unit you learn to…**

1. state a rule with the zero conditional
2. set a real condition with the first conditional
3. use unless, as long as and provided that
4. say when something will happen with time clauses

> **[FIGURE: `g-team`]** — *The Atlas Wire team — agreeing the conditions that must be met before anything runs.*

**Nothing runs until it is confirmed.** The Seven Crossings is written. Now come the conditions. Four newsrooms have agreed a single hour of publication, and a short list of things that must be true before that hour: two sources for every figure, a document for every claim, a right of reply for everyone named, and a lawyer's reading in each country. This week, Priya sets the conditions, Omar pushes to run early, and Mira learns to say *if* and *until* in a way nobody can misread. (Atlas Wire, Kalina Daily, the River Basin Network and the Meridian Post are invented, for practice.)

*A short scene to start the unit. Read it, then answer.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-meeting`]** — *The morning conference — the list of conditions goes on the wall.*

> "If a figure has one source, we do not publish it," Priya says. "That is the rule, and it does not change."
> Ana writes it on the board. "And if the Crossing Office gives us the method?"
> "Then we will run the figure on Sunday, with the method beside it."
> "And if it does not?"
> "We publish the story without the number. We do not publish a number we cannot stand behind."
> Omar's message arrives as she finishes. *If we wait, somebody else runs it first.* Ana reads it twice. "We will wait," she says, "until it is confirmed."

### PART 1 · The words of verification

*The words for conditions, proof and holding a story.*

> **[FIGURE: `u5-words`]** — *Four key words — condition, verify, embargo, second source.*

**The words**

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| condition | something that must be true first |
| verify | to prove that something is true |
| second source | another independent person who confirms it |
| corroborate | to support a claim with other evidence |
| evidence | the facts that prove something |
| document | a paper that proves something |
| embargo | an agreed time before which nothing is published |
| hold (v) | to wait before publishing |
| withhold | to keep something back |
| legal check | a lawyer's reading before publication |
| sign off | to approve for publication |
| right of reply | the chance to answer a claim about you |
| threshold | the level you must reach before you publish |
| provisional | not final; it may still change |
| independent | not controlled by anyone |
| risk (n) | the chance that something goes wrong |
| unless | if not |
| as soon as | immediately when |

### PART 2 · Grammar: rules and real conditions

*The zero conditional for rules; the first conditional for real futures; unless, as long as, provided that.*

> **[FIGURE: `u5-gA`]** — *Zero conditional = a rule that is always true. First conditional = one real future.*

> **1 · zero conditional — a rule**
>
> Form: {{If}} + present simple, present simple. "{{If}} a figure {{has}} one source, we {{do not publish}} it."
> For something always true: a rule, a law, a standing practice.
> You can swap the halves: "We {{do not publish}} a figure {{if}} it has one source."

> **2 · first conditional — one real future**
>
> Form: {{If}} + present simple, {{will}} + verb. "{{If}} the office {{confirms}} it, we {{will run}} it on Sunday."
> For one real possibility in the future, and its result.
> [[Never 'if…will']] in the if-half: say *if it confirms*, NOT *if it will confirm*.

> **[FIGURE: `u5-gB`]** — *unless = if not · as long as / provided that = only on this condition.*

> **3 · unless · as long as · provided that**
>
> {{Unless}} = if not: "We will not publish {{unless}} we have two sources."
> {{As long as}} / {{provided that}} = only on this condition: "We will run it {{as long as}} the method comes."
> [[Not with a second not]]: say *unless we have*, NOT *unless we don't have*.

> **[FIGURE: `u5-gC`]** — *Rule, real future, or condition — each has its own form.*

### PART 3 · Setting the conditions

*A conditions note says what must be true before publication, and when each thing happens.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-timezones`]** — *One hour, four countries. Every condition has to be met before it, not after.*

> **[FIGURE: `u5-skill`]** — *A conditions note: what must be true, who checks it, and by when.*

> **4 · time clauses — saying when**
>
> After {{when, until, as soon as, before, after, by the time}}, use the {{present}} for the future.
> "We will run it {{when}} the method {{arrives}}." "We will hold {{until}} it {{is}} confirmed."
> [[Not 'will' twice]]: say *as soon as it arrives*, NOT *as soon as it will arrive*.

**MODEL** — A model conditions note

> "Here are the conditions. If a figure has one source, it does not run — that is standing practice, not a judgement call. We will publish the Crossing Office number as soon as the method arrives; if it does not arrive by Friday, the story runs without it.
> Everyone named gets a right of reply, and we hold until the replies are in or the deadline passes. Each partner runs its own legal check. Nobody signs off before the two-source threshold is met.
> The embargo holds until 07:00 GMT on Sunday, unless all four of us agree to move it together."

**NOTICE** — Notice the conditions

> **[FIGURE: `u5-read`]** — *Conditions are not delays. They are the reason a story survives contact with the world.*

### PART 5 · Reading: the rules they agreed first

*Two readings. Read for the conditions, and for why they come before the calendar.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-reach`]** — *A story that runs in four countries can only be as strong as its weakest condition.*

**Reading A** · what must be true before Sunday

> **Nothing runs until it is confirmed**
>
> Before the four newsrooms agreed an hour, they agreed a list. It is one page long, it was written in a morning, and it is the reason the project will survive its own publication.
> The first condition is arithmetic. If a figure has one source, it does not run. "That is not a judgement we make story by story," says Priya Nair, who leads verification at Atlas Wire. "It is a rule. Rules are what you have when you are tired."
> The second is paper. Every claim about the crossings has to rest on something a reader could in principle see: a register, a council minute, a photograph with a date. Where a document exists but naming its keeper would put her at risk, the partners publish the document's substance and withhold her name.
> The third is the right of reply. Everyone named gets the chance to answer before publication, in their own language, with a real deadline. "If somebody answers us at the last hour, we will still carry it," says Omar Faris of the Meridian Post. "If they do not answer, we say that too."
> The fourth is law. Each partner runs its own legal check, in its own jurisdiction, because what is safe to print in one country is not always safe in another. Nobody signs off until all four have read the piece in their own jurisdiction.
> And then, last of all, comes the hour. The embargo holds until 07:00 GMT on the last Sunday of the month, and no partner may move it alone. "If a rival publishes first, we all move together, within the hour," says Ana Ferreira of Atlas Wire. "The one thing we never do is leave the smallest partner standing in the open on their own."

> **[FIGURE: `g-partners`]** — *The weakest partner sets the real deadline. That is not a weakness; it is the agreement.*

**Reading B** · the conditions, in short

> **Four conditions before you publish**
>
> **1. Two independent sources, or it does not run.** A rule, not a decision: *if a figure has one source, we do not publish it.* Rules survive tiredness.
> **2. Something a reader could see.** A register, a minute, a dated photograph. If naming its keeper would put them at risk, publish the substance and withhold the name.
> **3. A real right of reply.** Everyone named is asked before publication, with a deadline they can meet. If they answer late, carry it; if not, say so.
> **4. One hour, agreed by all.** Hold until the agreed time. If it breaks elsewhere, move together — never leave the smallest partner exposed.

### PART 8 · Ethics: holding and releasing

*An embargo is a promise to three other newsrooms. A condition is a promise to the reader.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-code`]** — *Independence is a condition too: nobody outside the newsroom sets the hour.*

> **[FIGURE: `u5-ethA`]** — *Running early wins one morning and costs three partners a day.*

**A first case** · the temptation to run early

> **A case.** Omar hears that a rival may have the story. If the Post runs on Saturday morning, it gets the credit and the traffic; if it waits, a competitor may take both. Nobody would be publishing anything false — only early. But three newsrooms built their Sunday around the agreed hour, and the smallest of them, Kalina Daily, has one front page a week and no second chance. An embargo is not a courtesy; it is the only thing that makes a partnership of unequal outlets possible. The Code says: a promise to a partner is a promise. What should Omar do if the rival publishes first?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

**A second case** · the condition that protects a person

> **[FIGURE: `u5-ethB`]** — *A document proves the claim. Naming its keeper can cost her everything.*

> **A case.** The far-bank account rests on a register kept for seven years by a woman on the closed side. The document is decisive, and Dren wants it published in full: it is his town, his scoop, and the proof of what people there lost. But her handwriting is on every page, and three people in the valley know whose it is. Atlas Wire can publish the substance and withhold her name, which is weaker journalism and a safer life. The pressure here comes from below, not above — and it is sincere. The Code says: no story is worth a source. What do the partners publish?

> **[FIGURE: `g-template`]** — *The assignment template — your conditions note.*

**Your task. **You are publishing a story with two partner newsrooms abroad. Write a conditions note (6–7 sentences). Give one standing rule (zero conditional), two real conditions and their results (first conditional), one condition with unless or as long as, and two time clauses saying when each step happens. End with what you will do if the story breaks elsewhere first.

> **[FIGURE: `g-model`]** — *A model — use Reading A and the Writing 1 model to check the shape of your note.*

> Remember: the zero conditional for rules; the first conditional for real futures (never 'if…will'); unless = if not; the present tense after when, until and as soon as; and nothing published that the conditions do not cover.

| Success criteria | Yes | Almost | Not yet |
|---|---|---|---|
| I state at least one rule in the zero conditional. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| I set real conditions in the first conditional, with no 'if…will'. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| I use unless or as long as correctly. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| I use the present after when, until and as soon as. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| Every condition is testable, and has a date. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |

## BOOK 2 · UNIT 6 · How Sure Are You? Writing About a Claim

**Beat · Verification & Across Borders**  ·  CEFR lower B1 → medium B1

**In this unit you learn to…**

1. say what is possible with might, may and could
2. say how likely something is
3. give advice with should and ought to
4. write about a claim you cannot prove yet

> **[FIGURE: `g-team`]** — *The Atlas Wire team — weighing a claim that nobody can prove, and that everybody is sharing.*

**A claim spreads across the basin.** A screenshot appears on Thursday evening. It says the gates of the upstream dam are going to be opened, and that the valley will flood within the week. By Friday morning it is in three countries, with no source, no date and no name. It might be true. It might be nothing. Thousands of people are frightened either way. This week, Priya traces it, Mira writes about it without repeating it, and four newsrooms learn how to say *we do not know* in a way that still helps. (Atlas Wire, Kalina Daily, the Meridian Post, the dam and the claim are invented, for practice.)

### PART 1 · The words of doubt

*The words for rumour, likelihood and careful reporting.*

> **[FIGURE: `u6-words`]** — *Four key words — rumour, unverified, plausible, speculation.*

**The words**

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| rumour | a story that spreads without proof |
| unverified | not yet proved |
| plausible | it sounds possible |
| likely | probable |
| unlikely | not probable |
| speculation | guessing without evidence |
| hedge (v) | to use careful words when you are not sure |
| caution | care, because something may be wrong |
| doubt (n) | the feeling that it may not be true |
| circulate | to pass from person to person |
| screenshot | a picture of a screen, often shared |
| origin | where something started |
| trace (v) | to follow something back to its origin |
| debunk | to show that a claim is false |
| flag (v) | to mark something as doubtful |
| correction | a published fix for an error |
| restraint | not publishing what you cannot prove |
| consequence | what happens because of something |

### PART 2 · Grammar: possibility and advice

*might, may and could for what is possible; should and ought to for what should be done.*

> **[FIGURE: `u6-gA`]** — *might · may · could — three ways to say 'possible, not certain'.*

> **1 · might · may · could — it is possible**
>
> Form: {{might / may / could}} + verb (no *to*, no *-s*). "The gates {{might be}} opened." "It {{may be}} genuine."
> All three say *possible*. {{May}} is a little more formal; {{could}} is often weaker.
> [[Not 'may to be']]: say *it may be true*, NOT *it may to be true*.

> **2 · saying it is not likely**
>
> Negative: "The valley {{may not}} flood." "It {{might not}} be genuine."
> [[Careful]]: *could not* usually means *was unable*, not *is not likely* — so for possibility use *may not* or *might not*.
> Questions: "{{Could}} the gates {{be}} opened without notice?"

> **[FIGURE: `u6-gB`]** — *should / ought to — what a newsroom owes its readers.*

> **3 · should · ought to — advice and duty**
>
> Form: {{should}} / {{ought to}} + verb. "We {{should}} say what we do not know." "A newsroom {{ought to}} publish a correction."
> For advice, and for a duty that is not a law.
> Negative: "We [[should not]] repeat the claim in the headline."

> **[FIGURE: `u6-gC`]** — *Possible, unlikely, or what we ought to do — each has its own form.*

### PART 3 · Writing about what you cannot prove

*You can report a claim without repeating it as a fact — if you are exact about what is known.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-sources`]** — *A claim with no origin is not a source. It is a thing that happened to the internet.*

> **[FIGURE: `u6-skill`]** — *Say what is claimed, who says it, what is confirmed, and what is not.*

**MODEL** — A model paragraph

> "A screenshot circulating since Thursday evening claims that the gates of the upstream dam will be opened this week and that the valley will flood. Atlas Wire has not been able to trace its origin, and no official body has issued such a notice.
> The Crossing Office says there is no plan to open the gates. That is not a denial that they could be opened in an emergency, and we have asked for one.
> Residents upstream have moved animals to higher ground. Whatever the claim turns out to be, that has already happened, and it is why we are reporting it."

**NOTICE** — Notice the paragraph

> **[FIGURE: `u6-read`]** — *Reporting a rumour is reporting its consequences — not repeating its words.*

### PART 4 · Listening: tracing the claim

*Two audios. Listen for what is possible, and for what a newsroom should do.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-desk`]** — *Audio 6.1 — verification looks for an origin, and does not find one.*

**Listening A** · looking for the origin

**MODEL** — Audio 6.1 — Priya and Mira

> **Priya:**  The earliest copy I can find is Thursday, 21:40, in a group of two hundred people.
> **Mira:**  Could that be the origin?
> **Priya:**  It might be. Or somebody may have copied it from somewhere we cannot see.
> **Mira:**  Is it plausible?
> **Priya:**  Partly. The dam does have gates, and they could be opened in an emergency. But the date in the message is wrong, and the logo is from an old document.
> **Mira:**  So it may be a real document, used wrongly?
> **Priya:**  That is the most likely explanation. We should say exactly that, and not more.
> **Mira:**  And the office?
> **Priya:**  They say there is no plan. They ought to say whether the gates could be opened at all.

### PART 5 · Reading: the claim that went upriver

*Two readings. Read for what was possible, and for the rules of a careful report.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-reach`]** — *A claim with no author reached three countries in twelve hours. The correction will not.*

**Reading A** · twelve hours, three countries

> **The screenshot that moved a valley**
>
> At 21:40 on Thursday, a message appeared in a group of about two hundred people upstream. It said the gates of the Vara dam would be opened within the week and that the lower valley would flood. It carried an official-looking logo and no name.
> By Friday morning it had reached three countries. "It was plausible, and that is the whole problem," says Priya Nair of Atlas Wire, who spent the day tracing it. "The dam does have gates. They could be opened in an emergency. Everything around the false part was true."
> Two things did not hold. The date in the message had already passed, and the logo came from a document issued four years ago. "Our best explanation is a real document used wrongly," Priya says. "It may have started as a warning between neighbours. We cannot prove that, so we have not written it."
> The Crossing Office said there was no plan to open the gates. Asked whether the gates could be opened without notice in an emergency, it did not answer. "That is not a denial," says Ana Ferreira of Atlas Wire. "A reader ought to be told the difference."
> Meanwhile, families upstream moved animals to higher ground, and a school kept its children indoors. Those consequences were real while the claim was not, which is why four newsrooms decided the story had to be reported — carefully, and without the claim in the headline.
> The piece they published said what was claimed, since when, by nobody traceable; what might be true; what the office would not say; and what families had already done. "We should be able to say *we do not know* in a way that still helps people," says Omar Faris of the Meridian Post. "That sentence is the hardest one in journalism."

**PRACTISE** — Comprehension

> **[FIGURE: `g-ladder`]** — *Four rungs from rumour to fact. You may report from the third; you can show from the fourth.*

**Reading B** · from rumour to fact

> **From rumour to fact: four rungs**
>
> **1. A rumour.** Somebody says it, and nobody can say who said it first. It might be true, and it is not yet reportable as a fact.
> **2. One source.** A person tells you directly, on the record. That is a claim with a name on it — still not a fact.
> **3. Two sources agree.** Two independent people who did not hear it from each other. Now you may report it, and say who.
> **4. A document.** A register, a notice, a dated photograph. Now you can show the reader what you saw.

### PART 8 · Ethics: giving a rumour oxygen

*Repeating a claim to deny it still carries it further. So does debunking a person instead of a claim.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-code`]** — *Accuracy includes accuracy about your own doubt.*

> **[FIGURE: `u6-ethA`]** — *A headline that repeats a claim spreads it, even with 'claim' in front.*

**A first case** · the headline that carries it

> **A case.** The Post's traffic desk points out, correctly, that 'Fears of flooding in the Vara valley' will be read ten times more widely than 'Unverified claim moves families upstream'. More readers would then see the careful paragraphs underneath. But most people read only a headline, and the first version plants exactly the belief the piece exists to correct. The claim gets the audience; the correction gets the few who scroll on. The first version would also be quoted back at the newsroom for a year. The Code says: a true sentence that leaves a false impression is not accurate. What headline should the partners run?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

**A second case** · debunking a person

> **[FIGURE: `u6-ethB`]** — *Debunk the claim. Naming the neighbour who forwarded it is not journalism.*

> **A case.** By Saturday, Dren has found the man who first posted the screenshot: a retired teacher upstream who believed it and sent it to a village group. Kalina Daily could name him, and the story would be strong — the origin, found, in a small town. But he invented nothing: he forwarded a real old document in fear, and he has neighbours who have already lost a great deal. Naming him would move the valley's anger from a claim to a person. Atlas Wire wants the origin in the copy; Dren wants his neighbour's name out of it. The Code says: debunk the claim, not the person. What do the partners publish?

### PART 11 · Assignment: a careful report

*Put the unit together: report a claim you cannot prove.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-template`]** — *The assignment template — your careful report.*

**Your task. **A claim is spreading and you cannot prove it. Write a careful report (6–7 sentences). Say what is claimed and since when, what you could not trace, what might or may be true, what an official body said and would not say, and what people have already done. Put the consequences in your headline, not the claim. End with one sentence about what your newsroom should do if it turns out to be wrong.

> **[FIGURE: `g-model`]** — *A model — use Reading A and the Writing 1 model to check the shape of your report.*

> Remember: might, may and could for possibility (no 'to'); may not or might not for 'not likely'; should and ought to for duty; the consequences in the headline; and the claim marked unverified.

| Success criteria | Yes | Almost | Not yet |
|---|---|---|---|
| I use might, may or could correctly for possibility. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| I use may not or might not for what is not likely. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| I use should or ought to for what the newsroom owes its readers. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| My headline is about consequences, not the claim. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| I say exactly what I could not confirm. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |

**Keep this. **In Unit 7, you write for the wire — the passive across tenses — because a wire sentence often has to say what was done before it can say who did it.

## BOOK 2 · UNIT 7 · For the Wire: Writing to Be Carried Everywhere

**Beat · Across Borders (wholly)**  ·  CEFR lower B1 → medium B1

**In this unit you learn to…**

1. form the passive in every tense
2. choose the passive when the action matters most
3. say by whom — and know when you must
4. write wire copy that any newsroom can carry

> **[FIGURE: `g-team`]** — *The Atlas Wire team — writing one sentence that two hundred newsrooms can publish unchanged.*

**One sentence, two hundred newsrooms.** This unit is wholly cross-border. A wire report is not written for one audience; it is written to be carried, translated and cut by newsrooms that have never seen the place. That is why so much of it is in the passive: *three crossings have been reopened*, *the figure is being checked*. The passive is a tool, and it is also a hiding place. This week, Mira learns to use it for clarity and to refuse it when somebody wants to use it to hide a name. (Atlas Wire, Kalina Daily, the Meridian Post and their staff are invented, for practice.)

| style guide | rules on writing names, numbers and dates |
| house style | one outlet's own rules |
| neutral | not taking a side |
| concise | short and clear |
| update (n) | a new version with new facts |
| kill (v) | to withdraw a story from the wire |

### PART 2 · Grammar: the passive

*be + past participle, in every tense; and when to name the doer.*

> **[FIGURE: `u7-gA`]** — *The passive puts the action first: 'three crossings have been reopened'.*

> **1 · the passive — the action first**
>
> Form: {{be}} + past participle. "The gates {{were opened}}." "The figure {{is checked}} twice."
> Use it when the action matters most, when the doer is unknown, or when the doer is obvious.
> Active: *The office reopened the crossing.* → Passive: The crossing {{was reopened}} (by the office).

> **2 · the passive across tenses**
>
> present: {{is / are}} checked · past: {{was / were}} opened · present perfect: {{has / have been}} reopened
> continuous: {{is / are being}} checked · future: {{will be}} carried · modal: {{can / must be}} used
> [[Watch the participle]]: say *has been reopened*, NOT *has been reopen*.

> **[FIGURE: `u7-gB`]** — *by + the doer: say it whenever you know it.*

> **3 · by whom — and when you must say it**
>
> Add {{by}} + the doer when the reader needs it: "The gates {{were opened by}} the Crossing Office."
> Leave it out only when it is unknown or obvious: "He {{was arrested}} yesterday."
> [[Never]] use the passive to hide a name you have: *mistakes were made* says nothing.

> **[FIGURE: `u7-gC`]** — *Action first, doer unknown, or a name being hidden — know which you are doing.*

### PART 5 · Reading: built to be carried

*Two readings. Read for how a wire sentence is made, and for the rules of the passive.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-reach`]** — *Written once, published two hundred times. Every weakness is published too.*

**Reading A** · how a wire sentence is built

> **Eleven words, two hundred newsrooms**
>
> A wire sentence is written to be used by people who will never meet its author. It will be translated into languages nobody in the newsroom reads, shortened to four paragraphs, and read by someone who has never heard of the river. That is why it is built the way it is.
> "Most of our leads are passive, and that is not laziness," says Daniel Okoye, world editor at Atlas Wire. "What has happened is usually what the reader needs first. *Three crossings have been reopened* — then the name of the body that reopened them."
> The name of the body is not optional, and never has been. A snap that says *the crossings were reopened* can be read as an accident of nature, and a sentence that can be read two ways will be, somewhere. So the authority goes into the first paragraph, because the first paragraph is sometimes all that is carried.
> Unfinished work is marked in the same grammar. *The figure of 112 returning families is still being checked* tells a subscriber in another country exactly how much weight to give the number, in six words. "The continuous passive is the most honest tense we have," Daniel says. "It says the work is still going on."
> Two things are never cut, in any version and at any length. The credit line names the outlet whose reporting it is, and the byline names the reporter who did it. Both were nearly lost when one subscriber's page template used agency bylines automatically.
> "A credit is not a courtesy," says Omar Faris of the Meridian Post, who had it corrected within the hour. "It is the only payment some reporters get, and in some places it is also their protection. A name on a story says somebody stands behind it."

**Reading B** · the passive on the wire

> **Four rules for the passive**
>
> **1. Use it when the action comes first.** *Three crossings have been reopened* puts the news where a reader starts. The body follows at once.
> **2. Name the doer whenever you have one.** Leave out *by* only when the doer is unknown or obvious. A passive with no name can be read as nobody's fault.
> **3. Mark unfinished work with the continuous.** *The figure is still being checked* stops a subscriber abroad printing a number as settled.
> **4. Never use it to hide.** *Mistakes were made* is grammar standing in for reporting. If you know who did it, the sentence says so.

### PART 8 · Ethics: the hiding place

*The passive can put the action first, or it can make a person disappear. The grammar is the same; the journalism is not.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-code`]** — *Independence means the grammar is chosen by the newsroom, not by whoever is named in it.*

> **[FIGURE: `u7-ethA`]** — *'Mistakes were made' is a sentence with nobody in it.*

**A first case** · the name the lawyers wanted out

> **A case.** Lawyers in two countries ask for the lead to read 'the crossings were reopened', with no body named. Their reasoning is reasonable: naming an authority invites a complaint, and the complaint lands on the smallest partner first. Nobody is asking Atlas Wire to write anything false. But a passive with no doer can be read as an accident, and the office's decision — taken by named people, announced on a Tuesday — becomes weather. If the sentence is wrong, nobody can even be asked about it. The Code says: the passive may order a sentence, never empty it. What goes in the lead?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

**8B**  Orders the sentence, or empties it? Write O or E.

1. 'Three crossings have been reopened by the Crossing Office.' ______
2. 'Mistakes were made in the figure.' ______

4. 'The credit was removed.' ______

**PRODUCE** — Discuss

**8D**  Discuss. Why does a complaint about a named authority usually land on the smallest partner first?

**A second case** · the credit that disappeared

> **[FIGURE: `u7-ethB`]** — *A template dropped three words. In Kalina, those three words are the story's spine.*

> **A case.** The Post's page template replaces partner credits with an agency line, automatically. Nobody decided to remove Kalina Daily's name; a system did, as it does every night. But Dren interviewed people on the closed side alone, and in his town the credit is both his pay and his standing — the proof that the work was his and that a large paper stands behind it. 'It was dropped by the system' is a true passive sentence with nobody in it. The Code says: a process is not an excuse; somebody owns it. What should the Post do, and what should Atlas Wire insist on?

## BOOK 2 · UNIT 8 · The Bigger Picture: Explaining Scale to a Distant Reader

**Beat · Explainer & Across Borders**  ·  CEFR lower B1 → medium B1

**In this unit you learn to…**

1. compare two things with comparatives
2. say which is the most with superlatives
3. use as…as, not as…as, too and enough
4. write an explainer for a reader who has never been there

> **[FIGURE: `g-team`]** — *The Atlas Wire team — turning seven crossings into one picture a distant reader can hold.*

**Explaining a place nobody has seen.** The Seven Crossings is reported. Now it has to be understood by someone two thousand miles away who has never heard of the river Vara. That is an explainer: scale, comparison, proportion. Which crossing is the busiest? Is the valley poorer than it was? Is a hundred and twelve families a lot? This week, Mira learns that a comparison is the most powerful sentence in an explainer — and the easiest one to get wrong. (Atlas Wire, Kalina Daily, the Meridian Post, the Vara basin and the figures in this unit are invented, for practice.)

### PART 1 · The words of scale

*The words for size, proportion and comparison.*

> **[FIGURE: `u8-words`]** — *Four key words — explainer, scale, proportion, benchmark.*

**The words**

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| explainer | a piece that explains the background of a story |
| scale (n) | how big something is |
| compare | to say how two things are different or alike |
| population | the number of people who live in a place |
| statistic | a number that describes a group |
| average | the usual or middle amount |
| per cent | out of a hundred |
| rate | how often or how fast something happens |
| proportion | one part compared with the whole |
| roughly | about; not exactly |
| significant | big enough to matter |
| benchmark | a figure you compare others against |
| equivalent | equal in value or size |
| misleading | giving a wrong impression |
| exaggerate | to make something sound bigger than it is |
| understate | to make something sound smaller than it is |
| far (adv) | by a large amount |
| slightly | by a small amount |

### PART 2 · Grammar: comparing

*Comparatives and superlatives; as…as and not as…as; too and enough.*

> **[FIGURE: `u8-gA`]** — *-er and more · the -est and the most.*

> **1 · comparatives — more than one other thing**
>
> Short words: busy → {{busier}}, small → {{smaller}} ({{than}}). Longer words: {{more}} important {{than}}.
> Irregular: good → {{better}}, bad → {{worse}}, far → {{further}}.
> Make it bigger or smaller: {{far}} busier, {{much}} smaller, {{slightly}} higher, {{a little}} worse.

> **2 · superlatives — the one above all**
>
> Short words: {{the busiest}}, {{the smallest}}. Longer: {{the most}} important.
> Irregular: {{the best}}, {{the worst}}, {{the furthest}}.
> Careful: "{{one of the}} busiest" is a claim you can prove; "{{the}} busiest" is a claim you must prove.

> **[FIGURE: `u8-gB`]** — *as…as · not as…as · too small · small enough.*

> **3 · as…as · too · enough**
>
> Equal: "Veren is {{as}} old {{as}} Kalina." Not equal: "It is {{not as}} busy {{as}} Kalina."
> {{too}} + adjective = more than is wanted: "The figure is {{too small}} to publish alone."
> adjective + {{enough}} = as much as is needed: "The case is {{clear enough}} to lead the piece."

> **[FIGURE: `u8-gC`]** — *Compare two, pick one from many, or measure against a need.*

**PRACTISE** — Structured practice

### PART 3 · Writing an explainer

*An explainer answers the question a distant reader cannot ask: is that a lot?*

> **[FIGURE: `g-ladder`]** — *Seven crossings, ranked. A ranking is a claim, so every step has to be defensible.*

> **[FIGURE: `u8-skill`]** — *An explainer gives the number, the benchmark, and the proportion.*

**MODEL** — A model explainer paragraph

> "There are seven crossings on the Vara. Kalina is the busiest: roughly two thousand people a week, more than the next two together. Veren is the smallest — eleven households — and the only one that has not reopened.
> A hundred and twelve families have returned to Kalina. That is far more than last year, when eleven came back, and far fewer than the nine hundred who left over the quiet years. In other words: the return is real, and it is about an eighth of what was lost.
> Eleven households sounds too small to matter. For Veren it is everything: it is the whole village."

**NOTICE** — Notice the explainer

> **[FIGURE: `u8-read`]** — *A number alone means nothing. A number with a benchmark means something.*

### PART 5 · Reading: seven crossings, compared

*Two readings. Read for the comparisons, and for the rules that keep them honest.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-reach`]** — *An explainer is read by people who will never see the place. Scale is all they have.*

**Reading A** · the basin, in proportion

> **Is a hundred and twelve a lot? The Vara basin in proportion**
>
> There are seven crossings on the river Vara, and almost nobody outside the valley could have named a single one of them a year ago. That is exactly the problem an explainer exists to solve.
> Kalina is the busiest. Roughly two thousand people cross it in a week — more than the next two crossings together, and about twenty times more than the quietest. "Busiest is a claim, so we checked it against the office's weekly counts," says Mira Sandoval of Atlas Wire. "If we could not prove it, we would have written *one of the busiest*."
> A hundred and twelve families have returned to Kalina since it reopened. On its own the figure means nothing. Last year, eleven families came back; over the quiet years, about nine hundred left. So the return is roughly ten times larger than last year's and roughly an eighth of what was lost. "Give both comparisons or neither," says Daniel Okoye, the world editor. "One of them alone is an argument, not a fact."
> Some comparisons were left out. The partners could not show that the valley is poorer than it was before the closure, because the figures are not good enough. "We can say the market is not as busy as it was," Mira says. "We cannot put a number on poverty here, so we do not."
> The smallest crossing is Veren: eleven households, and the only one of the seven that has not reopened. Eleven is too small for a chart, and the partners nearly cut it. In the end it led the piece. "The smallest number in the basin is the most important one," the explainer says, in the voice of Dren Markaj of Kalina Daily. "It is a whole village, and nothing has changed for it."

> **[FIGURE: `g-partners`]** — *Four newsrooms argued about one village of eleven households. It led the piece.*

**Reading B** · comparing honestly

> **Four rules for comparison**
>
> **1. Give both directions.** *Ten times more than last year, an eighth of those who left.* Either one alone is an argument.
> **2. Prove every superlative.** *The busiest* needs a source you can name. If you cannot prove it, write *one of the busiest* — almost as useful, and true.
> **3. Compare like with like.** Not a village against a city, or this April against a dry March. If they are less similar than they look, say so.
> **4. Never let size decide significance.** A number can be too small for a chart and large enough to lead. Eleven households is a whole village.

### PART 8 · Ethics: comparisons that mislead

*Every comparison is an argument. A true number inside a false comparison is still a false sentence.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-code`]** — *Accuracy includes the size of what you claim, not only the figures in it.*

> **[FIGURE: `u8-ethA`]** — *'The worst-hit valley in the region' is a superlative nobody has counted.*

**A first case** · the superlative nobody can prove

> **A case.** The Post's editors want a stronger line: 'the worst-hit valley in the region'. It would travel well, it would be quoted, and nobody could easily disprove it. The reporting supports something smaller, and firmer: Kalina is one of the worst-hit crossings on this river, by the office's own weekly counts. Nobody has counted the other valleys, so the bigger claim is not false exactly — it is unmeasured, which is worse, because a reader cannot tell the difference. The Code says: a superlative is a claim, and a claim needs a source. What line should run?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

**A second case** · the village that was too small

> **[FIGURE: `u8-ethB`]** — *A chart cannot hold eleven households. A newspaper can.*

> **A case.** Veren has eleven households, and the data team says it cannot be charted: the bar would be invisible beside Kalina's. The simplest decision is to cut it, and the argument is about scale, not politics — the piece is long, and eleven is a rounding error beside two thousand. But Veren is the only crossing of the seven that never reopened, which makes it the clearest case in the basin. Cutting it would leave a reader thinking the river had reopened everywhere. The Code says: do not let the size of a number decide whether people exist. What leads the piece?

### PART 11 · Assignment: an explainer

*Put the unit together: explain a place and its numbers to a distant reader.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-template`]** — *The assignment template — your explainer.*

**Your task. **Write an explainer (6–7 sentences) about a place or a figure in your own country, for a reader who has never been there. Use one superlative you can prove and name its source, two comparatives, one comparison in both directions, one 'not as…as', and one 'too…to' or '…enough'. End with one thing you cannot say, and why. If there is a small case the numbers would hide, put it first.

> **[FIGURE: `g-model`]** — *A model — use Reading A and the Writing 2 model to check the shape of your explainer.*

> Remember: -er / more…than; the -est / the most; 'one of the' when you cannot prove 'the'; both directions on every figure; too + adjective, adjective + enough; and never let size decide significance.

| Success criteria | Yes | Almost | Not yet |
|---|---|---|---|
| My comparatives and superlatives are correctly formed. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| Every superlative has a source, or becomes 'one of the'. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| I give both directions on at least one figure. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| I use as…as or not as…as, and too or enough, correctly. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| A small but telling case is not hidden by the numbers. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |

## BOOK 2 · UNIT 9 · Joining It Up: Co-Writing with Partners

**Beat · Co-Writing & Across Borders**  ·  CEFR lower B1 → medium B1

**In this unit you learn to…**

1. use quantifiers accurately (some, most, a few, several)
2. use a, an, the and no article correctly
3. join ideas with connectors
4. co-write one piece with two other newsrooms

> **[FIGURE: `g-team`]** — *The Atlas Wire team — merging three drafts into one piece that still tells the truth.*

**Three drafts, one piece.** Three newsrooms have written three parts of The Seven Crossings, and now the parts have to become a piece. Atlas Wire has the mouth of the river, the River Basin Network has the middle, and Kalina Daily has upstream. The facts agree. The voices do not, the quantifiers do not match, and in two places the accounts contradict each other. This week, Mira learns that joining writing up is mostly a matter of small words — *some*, *most*, *the*, *however* — and that the smallest words carry the most. (Atlas Wire, Kalina Daily, the River Basin Network and the Meridian Post are invented, for practice.)
