### PART 1 · The words of co-writing

*The words for merging drafts, voices and bylines.*

> **[FIGURE: `u9-words`]** — *Four key words — merge, version, seam, shared byline.*

**The words**

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| co-write | to write together |
| merge (v) | to join two texts into one |
| version | one of several forms of a text |
| track changes | a record of each person's edits |
| house voice | the way one outlet sounds |
| connector | a word that links sentences or clauses |
| transition | a phrase that carries a reader from one idea to the next |
| paragraph | a block of sentences on one point |
| structure (n) | the order of the parts |
| repetition | saying the same thing twice |
| overlap (n) | the part two texts both cover |
| seam | the place where two pieces join |
| consistent | the same all the way through |
| contradiction | two statements that cannot both be true |
| reconcile | to make two accounts agree |
| shared byline | a byline with more than one name |
| sign-off | the final approval |
| comment (n) | a note left on a draft |

### PART 2 · Grammar: the small words

*Quantifiers; a, an, the and no article; connectors.*

> **[FIGURE: `u9-gA`]** — *some · most · a few · several — each one is a different fact.*

> **1 · quantifiers — how many, how much**
>
> Countable: {{a few}}, {{several}}, {{many}}, {{most}}, {{all}}, {{none}} of the families.
> Uncountable: {{a little}}, {{much}}, {{most}} of the water, {{plenty of}} time.
> [[A quantifier is part of the fact]]: *some families returned* and *most families returned* are different claims.

> **2 · a, an, the — and no article**
>
> First mention: {{a}} crossing, {{an}} office. Second mention, or one we both know: {{the}} crossing.
> {{the}} with rivers and named things: {{the}} river Vara, {{the}} Crossing Office. No article with most place names: Kalina, Veren.
> [[Not 'the' for a general plural]]: say *families returned*, NOT *the families returned*, unless you mean particular ones.

> **[FIGURE: `u9-gB`]** — *however · although · because · so — the joints of a paragraph.*

> **3 · connectors — joining ideas**
>
> Contrast: {{however}} (new sentence), {{although}} / {{whereas}} (one sentence), {{but}}.
> Cause and result: {{because}}, {{since}}, {{so}}, {{therefore}}.
> Adding and sequencing: {{in addition}}, {{also}}, {{meanwhile}}, {{then}}.
> [[Punctuation]]: *However, the figure is unconfirmed.* — comma after *however*, not before a clause.

> **[FIGURE: `u9-gC`]** — *Quantifier, article, connector — the three joints of co-written copy.*

### PART 3 · Merging three drafts

*Co-writing is mostly joining: one voice, consistent quantifiers, and seams a reader cannot feel.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-pageflow`]** — *Three drafts in, one piece out. The joins are where the errors live.*

> **[FIGURE: `u9-skill`]** — *Merge in four passes: structure, quantifiers, articles, connectors.*

**MODEL** — A model merge note

> "Four passes. First, structure: Veren leads, then Kalina, then the middle crossings; each section keeps its reporter's byline.
> Second, quantifiers. Dren has 'most families' upstream; Ines has 'a few' in the middle. Both are right, so the piece says which crossings, and where. The Post's 'families have returned' goes — a missing quantifier is not neutral.
> Third, articles. It is 'the river Vara', 'the Crossing Office', but 'Kalina' and 'Veren' with no article.
> Fourth, connectors. However for contrast between sections, whereas inside a sentence, and nothing clever at the seams."

**NOTICE** — Notice the merge note

> **[FIGURE: `u9-read`]** — *A good seam is invisible. A bad one makes two true sentences look like a contradiction.*

### PART 5 · Reading: written by three, read as one

*Two readings. Read for the joins, and for the rules of co-writing.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-reach`]** — *One piece, three newsrooms, four countries — and it has to read as though one person wrote it.*

**Reading A** · how three drafts became one piece

> **The seams: co-writing The Seven Crossings**
>
> Three newsrooms wrote The Seven Crossings, and a reader should not be able to tell where one stopped and the next began. Getting there took four passes over three days, and almost none of the work was about facts. The facts had agreed with each other from the start.
> The first pass was structure. Veren, with eleven households, leads; Kalina follows; the middle crossings come third. "We argued for a day about the order and ten minutes about the facts," says Ines Duarte of the River Basin Network. "That is normal in co-writing."
> The second pass was quantifiers, and it was the dangerous one. Dren Markaj of Kalina Daily had written that most families upstream had returned. Ines had written that a few had. Both were correct, about different crossings, and side by side they looked like a contradiction. The piece now names the crossings in both sentences.
> Worse was a draft that had no quantifier at all: *families have returned*. "A missing quantifier reads as *all*," says Mira Sandoval of Atlas Wire. "Some is a fact. None is a hole, and the reader fills it."
> The third pass looked small: articles and names. The river Vara and the Crossing Office take *the*; Kalina and Veren take none. Three partners, two of them writing in a second language, had made eleven different choices between them, and a reader notices the eleventh even when they cannot say why.
> The fourth pass was the joins themselves, and it was the slowest. Contrast between sections is carried by *however*; contrast inside a sentence by *whereas*. Where Dren's account and Ines's disagree about a second ferry, nothing was smoothed: the piece says both, and says they disagree. "A seam you can feel is better than a seam that hides something," Ines says.

> **[FIGURE: `g-partners`]** — *Co-writing is an agreement about small words, made by people in different time zones.*

**Reading B** · co-writing with partners

> **Four rules for co-writing**
>
> **1. Agree the structure before the sentences.** Decide what leads, and in what order. Most arguments about style are arguments about structure.
> **2. Treat a quantifier as a fact.** *Most*, *some*, *a few* are not softeners; each is a different claim. Never delete one to tighten a sentence, or change one without asking its reporter.
> **3. Choose one house voice, and keep every byline.** One outlet's sound; every reporter's name, including the local one nobody could replace.
> **4. Do not smooth a real disagreement.** If two accounts differ, print both and say so. A visible seam is honest; a hidden one decides for the reader.

### PART 8 · Ethics: the small words

*Tidying is editing. Tidying away a quantifier, a byline or a disagreement is something else.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-code`]** — *Fairness lives in small words: which quantifier, whose name, whose account.*

> **[FIGURE: `u9-ethA`]** — *Deleting 'most' does not shorten a sentence. It enlarges a claim.*

**A first case** · the quantifier that was tidied

> **A case.** The Post's subeditor cuts 'most' from Dren's sentence, leaving 'families upstream have returned'. The motive is length: the line was one word over, and 'most' looked like a hedge. Nothing was invented, and no figure changed. But a sentence with no quantifier is read as *all*, and upstream some families have not come back and will not. Those families are now, in print, home. The person whose sentence it was was not asked, and he is the only one of the three who will meet them. The Code says: a quantifier is part of the fact. What happens before sign-off?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

**A second case** · the disagreement nobody wanted

> **[FIGURE: `u9-ethB`]** — *Two partners, two accounts. Printing both is harder and better.*

> **A case.** Dren says a second ferry ran last winter; Ines's sources say it did not. Both have notes, neither can prove it, and the point matters: if it ran, people had a way out that the official account denies. The easiest edit is to cut the sentence, and both partners would accept that — Dren because he is tired, Ines because it is not her section. A cut would leave the piece smooth, and would quietly settle a question in favour of the official version. The Code says: publish the disagreement you cannot resolve. What does the piece do?

*Put the unit together: join two accounts into one piece.*

**Your task. **With a partner, report the same event separately, then join the two accounts. Write a merge note and a joined paragraph (6–7 sentences). Agree the structure first. Use at least three different quantifiers, name the place each one applies to, use the and no article correctly with named things, and join your ideas with two connectors. Keep both bylines, and leave any real disagreement visible.

> **[FIGURE: `g-model`]** — *A model — use Reading A and the Writing 2 model to check the shape of your piece.*

> Remember: a quantifier is part of the fact; first mention a, second mention the; the river Vara but Kalina; one connector, not two; every byline kept; and a seam you can feel is better than one that hides something.

| Success criteria | Yes | Almost | Not yet |
|---|---|---|---|
| My quantifiers match the facts, and each names its place. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| My articles are correct with named and general things. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| I join ideas with single, correct connectors. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| Both reporters are credited. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| A real disagreement is printed, not smoothed. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |

**Keep this. **In Unit 10, the whole project goes out — gerunds and infinitives, and the capstone — because the last thing a cross-border piece needs is a plan for *publishing it*, and the will *to publish it* together.

## BOOK 2 · UNIT 10 · Across Borders: The Co-Production

**Beat · Capstone & Across Borders (wholly)**  ·  CEFR lower B1 → medium B1

**In this unit you learn to…**

1. use verb + -ing (gerunds) correctly
2. use verb + to + infinitive correctly
3. choose between -ing and to, and know when it changes the meaning
4. plan and publish a cross-border co-production

> **[FIGURE: `g-team`]** — *The Atlas Wire team on launch morning — one package, four countries, seven o'clock.*

**The co-production goes out.** This unit is wholly cross-border, and it is the capstone. At 07:00 GMT on the last Sunday of the month, four newsrooms publish The Seven Crossings: a long read, an audio piece, a subtitled film, a data page and seven photographs. Everything in this book is in it. What is left is the hardest part: deciding what to do after publishing, and agreeing to keep doing it. (Atlas Wire, Kalina Daily, the River Basin Network, the Meridian Post and everyone in the stories are invented, for practice.)

### PART 1 · The words of publishing together

> **[FIGURE: `u10-words`]** — *Four key words — co-production, package, launch, aftercare.*

**The words**

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| co-production | a piece made by several newsrooms |
| package | one story in several forms |
| launch (n) | the moment of publication |
| simultaneous | happening at the same time |
| localise | to adapt a piece for one audience |
| syndicate | to supply a piece to other outlets |
| licence (n) | permission to republish |
| credit line | the words naming every outlet |
| metrics | the numbers showing how a piece did |
| reach (n) | how many people saw it |
| impact | the change a story makes |
| follow-up | the next story after one |
| debrief (n) | a meeting to review what happened |
| aftercare | looking after sources after publication |
| moderation | managing readers' comments |
| transcript | the written version of audio |
| subtitle (v) | to add written words to a film |
| accountability | answering for what you publish |

### PART 2 · Grammar: -ing and to

*Verbs followed by -ing; verbs followed by to; and the ones that take both.*

> **[FIGURE: `u10-gA`]** — *Some verbs take -ing. Some take to. A few take both.*

> **1 · verb + -ing (the gerund)**
>
> After {{enjoy, avoid, finish, keep, suggest, consider, risk, mind, practise}}: "We {{finished checking}} the data."
> After every {{preposition}}: "before {{publishing}}", "instead of {{waiting}}", "good at {{explaining}}".
> As a subject: "{{Publishing}} together is harder than publishing alone."

> **2 · verb + to + infinitive**
>
> After {{decide, agree, promise, refuse, manage, offer, hope, plan, learn, intend, want}}: "We {{agreed to publish}} at seven."
> After adjectives: "It is hard {{to explain}}." With {{too}} / {{enough}}: "too late {{to change}}", "ready {{enough to launch}}".
> [[Not 'agree publishing']]: say *agreed to publish*, NOT *agreed publishing*.

> **[FIGURE: `u10-gB`]** — *stop doing · stop to do — the same verb, two different facts.*

> **3 · verbs that take both**
>
> No real change: {{start, begin, continue}} — "It {{started raining}}" = "It {{started to rain}}."
> A real change: {{stop}} {{-ing}} = end it; {{stop to}} = pause in order to.
> {{remember to}} = not forget; {{remember -ing}} = have a memory. {{try to}} = attempt; {{try -ing}} = experiment.

> **[FIGURE: `u10-gC`]** — *-ing, to, or both — know which verb you have.*

### PART 3 · Planning a co-production

*A co-production plan says what is being made, by whom, when it goes out — and what happens afterwards.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-partners`]** — *Four newsrooms, one package. The plan has to hold after publication too.*

**MODEL** — A model co-production plan

> "The package has five parts. Kalina Daily is writing the Veren section; the River Basin Network is making the audio; we are building the data page; the Meridian Post is editing the English and printing it. Everybody agreed to deliver by the 22nd.
> We intend to publish simultaneously at 07:00 GMT. Each partner may localise its own version, but nobody may change the credit line, and the licence keeps every name on every republication.
> After launching, we have promised to moderate the comments for a week and to hold a debrief on the Tuesday. Dren is going to the village at nine on Sunday morning. Nobody stops working when the piece goes out."

### PART 5 · Reading: seven o'clock, four countries

*Two readings. Read for the launch, and for what a newsroom owes after publishing.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-reach`]** — *Eleven million readers. Eleven households. Both numbers are the story.*

**Reading A** · the launch, and the morning after

> **Seven o'clock: publishing The Seven Crossings**
>
> At 07:00 GMT on the last Sunday of October, four newsrooms published the same investigation. The package had five parts: a long read, an audio piece, a subtitled film, a data page and seven photographs. By noon it had been republished by forty outlets, under a licence that keeps every partner's name on every copy.
> "Publishing together is much harder than publishing alone, and it is the only way this story could exist," says Ana Ferreira of Atlas Wire. "No single newsroom could have reported seven crossings in four countries. We needed to be four."
> The reach was eleven million. The partners had agreed to measure something else as well. "Metrics tell you who saw it," says Omar Faris of the Meridian Post. "They do not tell you what changed. We decided to publish a follow-up in the spring, before we knew whether we would want to."
> The hardest part began the next morning. Veren, the village of eleven households, had led the piece, and by Monday its residents were being telephoned by broadcasters in three countries. Only one journalist was there: Dren Markaj of Kalina Daily, who had agreed to go at nine on Sunday and was still going at six on Wednesday.
> "That is what aftercare means, and it is why we plan it before launching," he says. "Eleven million people finished reading and went to lunch. I live twenty minutes away."
> The debrief was held on the Tuesday. The partners agreed to extend moderation to three weeks, to pay for it jointly, and to correct an award entry submitted in one outlet's name. "The work is four newsrooms' work," Ines Duarte of the River Basin Network says. "So is the credit, and so is everything that comes afterwards."

> **[FIGURE: `g-credit`]** — *One licence, four names. The credit travels with every copy.*

**Reading B** · after you publish

> **Four rules for after publication**
>
> **1. Plan the aftercare before launching.** Who answers the phone, for how long, and who pays. The people in the story cannot move on.
> **2. Keep the credit on every copy.** Write the licence so republishing means keeping every name. A credit that survives syndication is worth most.
> **3. Measure what changed, not only who looked.** Metrics count readers; a follow-up asks what is different. Agree it before you know the answer.
> **4. Share everything that comes afterwards.** Awards, money, follow-ups and complaints belong to all the partners. If an entry carries one name, it is the wrong entry.

> **Mira:**  Thank you. And if they refuse?
> **Omar:**  Then we withdraw. I would rather explain withdrawing than explain the byline.
> **Mira:**  Dren said something similar. He would rather win nothing than see one name on it.

### PART 8 · Ethics: after the launch

*Publishing is the middle of the work. What a partnership does afterwards is what it was really worth.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-code`]** — *The Code does not end at publication. Neither does the partnership.*

> **[FIGURE: `u10-ethA`]** — *Eleven million readers moved on. Eleven households could not.*

**A first case** · the morning after

> **A case.** By Monday, broadcasters in three countries are telephoning Veren, and one family has been invited onto television. Nobody did anything wrong: the piece was accurate, fair and strong, and the attention is the consequence of its being read. But eleven households did not ask to become the most-read village in the basin, and the only journalist on the ground is Dren, who has a weekly paper to produce. Atlas Wire planned a week of moderation; three weeks is what the week after actually needs. The Code says: the duty starts at publication, it does not end there. What do the partners agree to do?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

**8A**  Choose (a) or (b), and write one reason.

1. (a) keep to the week that was planned  (b) extend moderation to three weeks and pay for it jointly.   Choice: ______  Because ________________________
2. Leaving the aftercare to the local partner is (a) practical  (b) passing the cost to the smallest newsroom.   Choice: ______

**8B**  Takes the duty, or passes it on? Write T or P.

1. 'We will extend moderation and pay from the joint budget.' ______
2. 'Our part is finished; the piece is published.' ______
3. 'Dren is there, so he can handle it.' ______
4. 'Two of us will share the calls this week.' ______

**PRACTISE** — Apply the Code

**8C**  Complete the rule. Use: before · afterwards · pays · starts.

> Plan the aftercare ______ launching. Say who ______ for it. Share everything that comes ______ . The duty ______ at publication.

**PRODUCE** — Discuss

**8D**  Discuss. Why does attention cost the smallest partner most?

**A second case** · the entry with one name

> **[FIGURE: `u10-ethB`]** — *An award with one name on it is a smaller thing than the work it is for.*

> **A case.** The Post's entry for a major award has gone in under its own name, because the form accepts only one outlet. The reasoning is administrative, not greedy, and the Post did most of the editing and all of the printing. But the Veren section was reported alone by a man who still lives there, the audio was made in another country, and the data page took three weeks. An award is a record of who did the work, and this one would be wrong for ever. The Code says: the credit is the partnership's, or it is nobody's. What should the partners do if the form cannot take four names?

**NOTICE** — What do you do?

**8E**  Choose (a) or (b), and write one reason.

1. (a) let it stand — the form only takes one  (b) ask for the form to change, and withdraw if it cannot.   Choice: ______  Because ________________________
2. An entry under one name is (a) an administrative detail  (b) a permanent record that is wrong.   Choice: ______

**8F**  Complete with: form · withdraw · record · alone.

1. The ___________ accepts only one outlet.
2. Dren reported the Veren section ___________ .
3. An award is a ___________ of who did the work.
4. If the form cannot change, the partners will ___________ .

**PRODUCE** — Discuss

**8G**  Discuss. Why would Dren rather win nothing than see one name on the entry?

**PRODUCE** — Write it

**8H**  Write two sentences to an awards body asking it to accept four names. Use an infinitive and a gerund.

**PRACTISE** — One more

**8I**  Shares the work's credit, or takes it? Write S or T.

1. 'The entry goes in under all four names.' ______
2. 'We entered it ourselves; we did the editing.' ______
3. 'The licence keeps every name on every copy.' ______
4. 'Our masthead is the one readers know.' ______

**8J**  Discuss. A partnership of unequal newsrooms published one piece. What makes it equal, in the end?

### PART 11 · Final project: your co-production

*Bring the whole of Book 2 together. Plan and publish a cross-border co-production.*

> **[FIGURE: `g-template`]** — *The template — build your co-production part by part.*

**Your task. **Plan a co-production with two partner newsrooms abroad, on a story of your choice. Work alone or in a small team — a coordinator, a reporter and an editor. Write the plan, one section of the package, and the launch post.

> **[FIGURE: `g-frontpage-parts`]** — *Every part of the package, and what each one is for.*

**Your co-production must have:**

1. a **recap**, in the present perfect and the past simple — Unit 1;
2. a **backstory** with used to, would and the past continuous — Unit 2;
3. a **plan** with going to and every hour in every time zone — Unit 3;
4. one **exact quote in reported speech**, with say, tell or according to — Unit 4;
5. the **conditions** for publication, in the zero and first conditionals — Unit 5;
6. one **careful paragraph** about something unproved — Unit 6;
7. a **wire lead** in the passive, naming the body that acted — Unit 7;
8. an **explainer** sentence with a provable superlative — Unit 8;
9. **quantifiers, articles and connectors**, joining three accounts — Unit 9;
10. a **launch post** and an **aftercare plan** — Unit 10.

> **[FIGURE: `g-model`]** — *A model — use Reading A and the Writing 1 model to check the shape of your project.*

> Before you publish, agree the conditions. Check every figure twice, keep every quantifier, name every partner, and plan the morning after. Hold the hour you promised. Then publish — together, within the hour. That is the whole of Book 2, on one page.

| Success criteria — the whole book | Yes | Almost | Not yet |
|---|---|---|---|
| My plan names every partner, every part and every hour with its time zone. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| My conditions are testable, and the aftercare is agreed before the launch. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| Every quote is reported accurately, and every figure is attributed. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| Every unproved claim is marked, and every superlative can be proved. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| The credit line carries every partner's name, on every copy. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |
| The smallest partner can meet the plan, and is not left alone afterwards. | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |

**Congratulations. **You have finished English for Journalists, Book 2. You began by recapping one story for a colleague abroad; you can now plan, report, write, verify and publish journalism made by newsrooms in four countries — in English, as an equal partner, and with a journalist's care for the people in the story. A free press, without borders.

Atlas Wire, Kalina Daily, the River Basin Network, the Meridian Post, their staff, Dren Markaj, Veren, the Vara basin, The Seven Crossings and every figure in it are invented, for practice.
